# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical Read: "Two Years On" (Varden 24-Month Follow-up and Halden Subset)

**Bottom line:** This is the most informative document in the set. It answers the open questions directly: whether the gain lasts, what explains it, whether timesheets missed work, and what happens in coverage-bound work. It also meets the standards that Varga & Holm and the meta-analysis set out. Its central findings hold up:

- the per-hour gain shrank but persisted at two years, at about 8.5–10%;
- output per employee sits slightly below control, at about −3%;
- coverage-bound reduced hours could not be sustained without extra staff;
- the reduction in meetings is the largest identified pathway.

The main problems are these:

- the Summary compares figures from two different hours measures, which makes the decline look bigger than it is;
- a **control-group contamination** event that the authors report but never connect to the decline they observe;
- a mediation test run on the same offices that generated the hypothesis;
- the cost of case-processing is still missing.

## The numbers check out

- Output per hour, timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, so **+9.8%**. Logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, so **+8.5%**.
- Meeting change relative to control: (3.9 − 7.4) − (7.0 − 7.2) = **−3.3 hours/week**. This matches the 9-month cross-sectional gap.
- Mediation shares sum to 100% (47 + 18 + 35).
- Halden continuers: 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, and 96.8 / 0.866 = 1.118, so **+11.8%**.

## What it does well

- **It tests the earlier claims rather than defending positions.** The mediation analysis was registered before the 24-month outcomes. A stricter hours measure (system logs) was added. The Halden figures are explicitly labelled as survivors twice over.
- **It resolves the timesheet concern.** Logs show slightly more work than timesheets, but the difference is small (11% vs 12%).
- **It establishes a baseline for meetings.** Pre-period meeting data now exist, which fixes the weakness in the 9-month exploratory analysis. (The paper should say how these were obtained, presumably from calendar history, since the original protocol collected them only in month six.)
- **It reports the decline even though it weakens the authors' earlier result.** The 9-month estimate of 12.5% shrank to 9.8%.
- **It gives a fair verdict on both earlier critiques.** Varga & Holm were right about inflated headline figures but wrong about "entirely an artifact." The meta-analysis's four long studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That fully confirms the earlier concern that its duration claim could not show an absence of decline.
- **It reports the counter arm against control.** The waits are now 7.3 vs 4.0 minutes (earlier they were reported only before-and-after), with a staffing and cost estimate.
- **It is honest about what it can't determine.** The paper notes that no arm reorganised without also reducing hours.

## Problems

### 1. The Summary compares two different hours measures
The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But 12.5% is a timesheet figure and 8.5% is a log figure.

The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8%, a fall of about 22%. The cross-measure comparison suggests about 32%. The body of the paper and §5 ("about a quarter") use the right comparison; the Summary should too. The 9-month figure on a log basis is unknown and was probably somewhat below 12.5%.

### 2. The decline is not tested statistically
The confidence intervals at 9 and 24 months overlap substantially (6.9–18.4 vs 4.6–15.2). Because these are the same offices, a direct test of the change is possible but not reported.

The body's wording, "consistent with some fading," is appropriately cautious. §5's "declined by about a quarter" states the decline as established fact.

### 3. Control-group contamination may explain part of the "decline"
Two control offices cut their meetings in month 15 and gained about 4.1% in output per hour. This improves the control arm, which mechanically shrinks the gap between treated and control.

Rough illustration: if all offices were similar in size, two of seven control offices gaining 4.1% raises the control average by about 1.2 points. That could account for something like 40% of the 2.7-point decline. Some of the apparent fading may therefore reflect control offices catching up, not treated offices slipping.

The authors present the meeting audit only as evidence about mechanism. They never connect it to the decline estimate. They should report the estimate with those two offices excluded, or from before month 15.

There is also an arithmetic puzzle. If two offices fell by about 2.1 hours each, the control mean should drop by about 0.6 hours. Yet it fell only 0.2 (7.2 → 7.0), which implies the other control offices increased their meeting time. Possible, but worth explaining.

### 4. The mediation test is not an independent replication
Registration at month 11 prevents choosing the analysis to fit the results. But the hypothesis came from these same seven treated offices. Months 0–9 contribute to both the exploratory finding and the "confirmatory" test.

"Survives a registered test" is accurate. Calling it confirmation of an independent hypothesis is not.

### 5. "A larger sample of office-months" overstates the evidence
The independent units are still 7 treated and 7 control offices. Adding months adds precision within each office, but not independent evidence across offices. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters, and the paper should confirm that the analysis is clustered at the office level.

The usual causal assumptions behind mediation also apply. Randomisation assigned the hours, not the meeting cuts. Offices with better managers may both cut more meetings and produce more. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary's word "confirms" doesn't reflect it.

### 6. Simple accounting suggests meetings could explain even more
A back-of-envelope calculation, assuming control hours of about 37.9 and that meeting time produced no output:

| | Log hours | Meetings | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | ~37.9 | 7.0 | ~30.9 |
| Treated | ~33.7 | 3.9 | ~29.8 |

Non-meeting time fell about 3.6%. Output fell 3.4%. So output per non-meeting hour is almost unchanged.

On this accounting, removing meetings explains nearly the whole per-hour gain, not 47%. The two approaches answer different questions. Mediation asks how much of the variation between offices tracks meeting cuts. Accounting asks how much time was removed. Meetings also may have had some real value. Still, the authors should reconcile the two. Taken together, they point toward reorganisation mattering more than rest.

### 7. Case-processing cost is still unreported
Output per FTE is −3.4% at full pay, so labour cost per case rose by at least about 3.5%, plus any overtime premium. The paper prices the counter arm (+9% per contact) but not the arm that continues. For the county's decision, this is the most important missing number.

### 8. The Halden reversions are framed too neatly
The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations." Two had genuine coverage obligations (retail and hospitality). The third was a marketing agency citing client deadlines, which is closer to discretionary work. That is a counter-example to the coverage-bound explanation, and the framing smooths it over.

Other points on the Halden subset:
- 9 of the 23 organisations with records did not respond, and non-response is probably worse among poor performers.
- The 40.3-hour baseline appears to be the 27-organisation figure from Varga & Holm, not the baseline for these 11 organisations.
- It is unclear whether all 11 have time tracking.
- Without a comparison group, "upper bound" is reasonable but not guaranteed, since trends over two and a half years could run either way.

### 9. Minor points
- **Conflict of interest.** A Halden author (Okafor) co-authors the section on Halden organisations. It is handled candidly, but should be disclosed.
- **Resignations** (4.1% vs 7.9%) are still reported without a confidence interval.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Question | Status after this report |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | **About 8.5–10% at 24 months** (randomised, records, logs), down from about 12.5% at 9 months; part of the decline may be control contamination |
| Output per employee, discretionary work | About −3% (CI includes zero), so cost per case is higher |
| Coverage-bound work | **Not sustainable as designed**: arm stopped, waits nearly doubled, about +9% cost to restore service |
| Durability | Gain persists at 2 years in one employer; "no decay" (meta-analysis) and "entirely artifact" (Varga & Holm) both rejected |
| Mechanism | Meeting reduction is the largest identified pathway (about half, possibly more); fatigue is smaller (about a fifth). Halden's fatigue-first explanation is not supported |
| Can reorganisation alone deliver the gain? | **Untested.** Two-office anecdote only |

## A fair summary

In one public employer's case-processing offices, a randomised cut to 30 scheduled hours produced an 11–12% fall in actual hours. Output per hour was about 8.5–10% higher than control at two years, and output per employee was about 3% lower, so cost per case was somewhat higher. The gain shrank from nine months, though part of that may reflect control offices adopting meeting cuts.

The largest identified contributor is the removal of recurring meetings; reduced fatigue plays a smaller role. Reduced hours in counter work worsened service and were abandoned. The decisive next study is a three-arm trial:

1. reduced hours;
2. structured meeting and workflow reform at normal hours;
3. control.

That design would show whether the gain comes from the shorter week itself or from the reorganisation it prompts.
